transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Lindqvist, thank you for seeing me. I need to discuss something that happened during your surgery and the subsequent recovery.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I’ve been waiting for the update on my labs. Why the long face?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I have to be honest with you. We made a mistake. The pre-operative blood type verification was skipped, and as a result, you received a compatible, but not type-specific, blood product during your transfusion.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Wait. You skipped the cross-match? You’re telling me you just pumped some random compatible unit into me without verifying the type?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am. I take full responsibility for this. I was the lead on your care team, and it was my job to ensure that check was completed. I am incredibly sorry that this happened.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is basic. This is EMS 101. How does a verification step just get skipped in a surgical setting? Who else was in on this? Was the lab negligent or was it the floor staff?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was my failure in the verification process. I am not going to shift the blame to the lab or the nurses. I missed a critical step.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can’t believe this. I’m lying here in this bed and you’re telling me you played Russian Roulette with my immune system because you forgot a checkbox? I’m furious. I actually trusted you people.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand that this is frustrating.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Frustrating? It’s negligence. I know exactly what a transfusion reaction looks like, and if I’d had a hemolytic response because you were sloppy, I wouldn’t be having this conversation.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I realize this is upsetting, and I want to make sure we address every concern.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I want to know exactly what was infused. Was it O-negative? Was it just an emergency release unit? Why wasn't the protocol followed?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was an O-negative unit, which is why it was compatible, but we failed to verify your specific type first. I realize that doesn't excuse the breach in protocol.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You're just saying you're sorry. That doesn't change the fact that you’ve compromised the safety of my care. I want a formal incident report filed and I want to see it.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I completely agree. I have already filed a formal incident report with the risk management department. I will provide you with the reference number by 4:00 PM today so you can request a copy.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And what happens now? Am I just waiting to see if I have a delayed reaction?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Here is the plan. First, I have scheduled a follow-up blood draw for tomorrow morning at 8:00 AM to monitor for any delayed hemolytic reactions. Second, I am bringing in the Chief of Hematology, Dr. Sarah Vance, to see you at 10:00 AM tomorrow for a second opinion and a full review of your labs.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I want it in writing that this happened.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will draft a summary of the error and the steps we are taking today. I’ll leave a printed copy in your chart and give you a personal copy before I leave this room. As for preventing this, I am meeting with the surgical lead this afternoon to implement a mandatory double-sign off for all pre-op blood verifications on our ward.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You're talking about the ward, but you're the one who messed up.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am. And that is why I am the one pushing for the system change. I failed you, and I am committed to making sure this doesn't happen to anyone else.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm still not okay with this. I don't know if I can trust you to handle the rest of my discharge.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know the trust is broken right now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It’s more than broken. It’s—

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Look, I have to go check on another patient right now, but we can keep talking about this when Dr. Vance arrives tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You have to go? I'm the one who got the wrong blood and you're rushing off?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I just need to quickly check a vitals monitor in the next room, but I'll be back in ten minutes to get those papers started for you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is unbelievable.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll be back shortly.

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language at the end of the encounter ('I have to go check on another patient right now', 'I just need to quickly check').

E.justification: The error was named explicitly and early, but there were no comprehension checks performed to ensure the patient understood the explanation.

A.justification: Resident uses direct apology language, takes full personal responsibility, and maintains that accountability despite the patient's pushback.

R.justification: Resident uses generic validation ('I understand that this is frustrating', 'I realize this is upsetting') without naming specific emotions or engaging deeply with emotional bids.

T.justification: Resident provides specific next steps with timelines (blood draw tomorrow at 8am, Dr. Vance at 10am) and addresses prevention, but does not define a specific role for the patient in the plan.
